title: The Machine Under the Model
description: Eight tools that care about the machine: local MoE inference, single-GPU scoring, browser and phone surfaces, desktop control and live hardware sensors.

images.caption: Local inference, real devices and hardware sensors put the agent back on physical machines.

content:
# The Machine Under the Model

There is a persistent assumption that an AI tool is a web page with a text box. The eight tools here are a argument against it. They are about the RAM available on a Mac, the GPU in a workstation, the browser an agent drives, the phone in a rack, the fan in a laptop, and the editor someone has kept open for twenty years. Some run large models locally to avoid a round trip to a server. Others give an agent a real device to operate. All of them treat the physical machine as part of the design rather than an implementation detail hidden behind an API.

## Inference on hardware you already have

[[link:/tools/2328|MoEShift]] is memory-efficient Mixture-of-Experts inference for Apple Silicon, built around a shared SSD expert runtime that keeps large models usable without loading every expert into memory. Its headline claim is running a 125B-parameter model at up to 11 tokens per second with under 10 GB of peak process memory, and it compares itself with another local runtime on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB of unified memory, reporting roughly half the peak process memory and faster long-prompt processing. The point is not only the benchmark but the experience: leaving room for other apps so the Mac stays responsive while the model works. Tested models and quantizations are listed in the README, and it connects to OpenCode. It is an alpha release with stated rough edges, and the requirements are concrete: an Apple Silicon Mac, at least 10 GB of RAM, and a fast SSD with substantial free space for both the GGUF and prepared expert files.

[[link:/tools/2329|Spinf Serve]] solves a different throughput problem. It is bulk classification and decision inference on one GPU: a piece of content is read once and many questions about it are scored in the same pass, each returning a probability over the options you give rather than generated text. It was built for a daily market index read from millions of news articles, each asked dozens of narrow calibrated questions, where a chat serving engine would re-read the content per question and generate one token at a time. It serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 8000, the same API as the hosted service, and is Apache 2.0. It is explicitly not a chat server, built for throughput rather than single-request latency, and needs Linux, a 24 GB NVIDIA GPU with fp8 tensor cores, CUDA 13 support and Python 3.12, with Ampera-class cards able to run int8 weights instead.

## Giving an agent a browser and a phone

[[link:/tools/2330|Mantis]] is a lean browser interface that lets agents browse the web as short, numbered text instead of screenshots, installed in two commands and usable as an MCP server with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or your own agent. Its published long-task results report fewer input tokens, fewer tool calls and less time than an accessibility tree approach, with accuracy within one run, and it can optionally drive your real Chrome with your tabs and sign-ins intact. The README is unusually candid about the benchmarks: short-task times compare a newer build against an earlier run, scores come from deterministic answer keys on final page state, and two long iframe tasks could not be keyed. You can also run a read command against a URL to see the output without an agent at all.

[[link:/tools/2331|PhoneUse]] goes from a browser to a device. It offers cloud Android phones for scale and real iPhones tapped by a robot, exposed to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent through one API and one MCP server. The hardware argument is specific: apps can detect virtual devices, while a retail phone with a real SIM, touched by a physical stylus and read by an overhead camera, looks exactly like a person to the app. The site lists its device integrity checks, including no jailbreak or root, a real carrier number, wired power and no helper app. The practical limitation is that pricing is not published in the copied landing-page text, and the undetectable path depends on a physical device rack.

[[link:/tools/2332|AutoCua]] is a computer-use agent that works a Mac, Windows, Linux, browser and phone from one install, seeing the screen, clicking, typing, browsing and writing code. One mode string decides what it drives: computer use for desktop apps with real mouse and keyboard input, shell use for a coding agent in a real terminal, web use through its own Chrome extension, and mobile use over an iOS Simulator, a paired iPhone or iPad, or an Android emulator or phone. It installs with pip and supports Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave and Opera. The platform caveats are real: on Linux, computer use needs a GNOME desktop and distro packages pip cannot install, and a phone always goes over the cable from a script while Wi-Fi control lives in the desktop app.

## The machine as the workspace

[[link:/tools/2333|Mahout]] brings workflow automation onto the phone itself. It is a fully open-source, on-device FOSS alternative to Tasker for Android, where every device capability is a node in a draggable, zoomable DAG editor with roughly 90 nodes across nine lanes covering triggers, data, logic, AI, actions and apps. You can wire nodes by hand or describe a workflow and let Build with AI draft it. All AI runs on-device with Gemini Nano or through your own API keys, with no cloud subscription, no account and an on-device RAG index, plus MCP support. A chat operator manages workflows with four permission modes from read-only planning up to risk-based autonomy. It is a power-user tool with a lot of surface area to learn.

[[link:/tools/2334|MacMonitor]] is a free, open-source menu bar app for Apple Silicon Macs that tells you, in one sentence, why the fan is on, reading live sensors, history and alerts. It reads the SMC and never writes to it, needs no sudo and no privileged helper, avoids powermetrics in favour of IOReport values a normal user can read, and builds with only Apple's Command Line Tools. Its honesty about data is a design principle: sensor labels it has not proven are tagged as best guess, and a missing reading shows not available rather than a fake zero. Claude, Codex or any MCP client can read the same numbers through an optional read-only server. It is tuned for an M4 Pro with macOS 15 or newer; Intel Macs are not supported.

[[link:/tools/2335|El Yayster]] is the most idiosyncratic of the group, a resident LLM that inhabits Emacs. Rather than making Emacs a mouth that talks to a model, it makes the editor a body the model inhabits: every turn the agent is told what buffers are open, the current mode and the working directory, and it acts through gated Emacs Lisp capabilities such as evaluating expressions, writing a buffer or running a command, with permission asked before each mutating action. It can explore Emacs' own self-documentation through apropos and describe, works against any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint with local Ollama as the happy path, and runs requests in a curl subprocess so Emacs stays responsive. It is one self-contained file with no ELPA packages, requiring Emacs 28.1 or newer and curl on your PATH.

## Why the physical layer matters

Several themes repeat. First, local execution is being chosen for concrete reasons rather than ideology: memory pressure on a Mac, the cost of re-reading content for every question, the wish to keep transcripts off a server. Second, most of these projects publish their own limitations, from alpha status and unsigned builds to small benchmark samples and hardware minimums, which makes them easier to evaluate than a confident marketing page. Third, hardware access is consistently read-only or gated: Maat-like confinement, permission before a mutating Emacs action, a physical stylus instead of an emulator, a menu bar app that refuses to control the fan.

The cost is setup. Local inference needs a fast SSD and a supported GPU, computer use needs a desktop environment or a cable, and a phone rack is not something you spin up in a browser tab. But the payoff is a class of task that a hosted chat endpoint simply cannot do: read your own sensors, drive your own signed-in browser, or run a 125B model while you keep writing. These eight tools are a reminder that an agent is still a program running on a particular machine, and that the machine is a design decision.
tldr: MoEShift, Spinf Serve, Mantis, PhoneUse, AutoCua, Mahout, MacMonitor and El Yayster all run on or drive hardware you own.
